text: Filing, searching, filtering, commenting on, and managing GitHub issues. That's the headline. The real work underneath is building judgment: which issues matter, which ones can wait, and how you verify the outcome actually worked.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So we're not skipping the written material. We're using audio to lower the barrier to entry and stick with you longer.

speaker: ALEX
text: Filing, Managing, and Participating in GitHub Issues. This is where open source collaboration actually starts. The concrete skill layer: everything from discovering the right issue to writing a bug report that maintainers can act on - all navigable with your keyboard and screen reader.

speaker: ALEX
text: Here's the working method: read the title first, then the body, then scan the timeline. You're listening for three things - what action is being requested, what evidence is missing, and who needs to jump in next.

speaker: ALEX
text: Now, the learner layer. Chapter 5 is the first challenge chapter built around issues, with small, confidence-building tasks. It covers Challenge 2 - Create Your First Issue - and Challenge 3 - Join the Conversation. speaker: ALEX
text: Three anchors: there are two main challenges plus one optional add-on. Each one fits within ten minutes. Your work appears as comments and issue details. The rhythm is: propose something, do it, confirm it worked.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What does someone do first, second, and after that?

speaker: ALEX
text: Chapter 5 focuses specifically on issue skills. This matters because you won't need to create branches or edit files for any of these tasks.

speaker: ALEX
text: Go in sequence: first you create an issue with clear language and specifics; next you leave a comment on someone else's issue and tag them with an @mention; last, if the feature is available, you can break a bigger issue into smaller tracked sub-issues. Every move leaves evidence you can point to later.

speaker: JAMIE
text: That's clearer when you hear it as one connected piece.

speaker: ALEX

speaker: JAMIE
text: Give us the walkable path.

speaker: ALEX
text: Start with Challenge 2 Step-by-Step: Create Your First Issue. File a new issue in your Learning Room repository - one with a thoughtful title and a real description. Here's the part that matters: issues are the prompts that wake up AI agents.

speaker: ALEX
text: For people learning this, concrete examples are the guides. "Agent Request: Add missing contributor background paragraph in welcome.md". "Keyboard shortcuts table has incorrect NVDA modifier key". "Setup guide link to accessibility settings is broken". These say what the problem is or what content is missing.

speaker: ALEX
text: Here's the startup sequence: open your Learning Room repository in your browser; navigate to Issues (keyboard shortcut G then I, or find the "Issues" link in the nav); activate New issue; and if a template picker shows up, select Open a blank issue or pick a template if it fits. If something doesn't match, stop and recalibrate.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What's the actual workflow?

speaker: ALEX
text: Once you name it, it becomes simple. In the Title field, write something specific - at least 12 characters. In the Body field, write a real description - at least 80 characters. Hit Submit new issue. Copy the issue URL or write down the number - for example, 150. You'll use that reference later. Every move should show itself.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Walk me through Challenge 3 Step-by-Step: Comment and @Mention next.

speaker: ALEX
text: The sequence is this: find an issue someone else opened and add a comment using an @mention to get their attention. Here's what that looks like in practice. "@classmate I can confirm this - the link in setup-guide.md goes to a 404 page.". "@classmate Good catch! I think the correct shortcut is Insert+F7, not Insert+F5.". "@classmate I'd suggest adding the paragraph right after the 'Who Can Contribute' heading.".

speaker: ALEX
text: The move breaks down this way. Open the Issues tab in your Learning Room; scan for an issue a classmate wrote, or use one the facilitator provided; open that issue by clicking its title; read the description so you understand what they reported. That's how you get your bearings.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Then what?

speaker: ALEX
text: Scroll to the comment box at the bottom. Type a thoughtful comment that @mentions them by username. Activate Comment - or use Ctrl+Enter. The pause between each action is what keeps complex workflows from unraveling.

speaker: ALEX
text: The winning habit is straightforward: understand your surroundings, take your action, verify the result, move forward. That moment of pause - where you check what changed - is part of the actual work, not a delay before it.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Let's talk about Optional Extension Step-by-Step: Add a Sub-Issue. What sticks with a learner?

speaker: ALEX
text: Don't treat Optional Extension Step-by-Step: Add a Sub-Issue as nice-to-have decoration. This is about taking a large issue and chopping it into smaller, tracked pieces using GitHub's sub-issue feature. It's a real skill.

speaker: ALEX
text: For example: sub-issue - "Add alt text to welcome banner image". Sub-issue - "Fix heading hierarchy in Getting Started section".

speaker: ALEX
text: The process: open the issue you made in Challenge 2 or any open issue you can edit; look for the Sub-issues section in the sidebar on the right; if you don't see it, find Add sub-issue or Create sub-issue option below the description; activate Add sub-issue and choose Create new sub-issue; give it a focused title describing one specific piece of the parent work.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What's the payoff?

speaker: ALEX
text: Add a short description, then activate Create. The sub-issue appears nested under the parent with a progress tracker. Every action produces a visible confirmation, which is what makes workflows reliable.

speaker: JAMIE
text: How does someone prove they've finished?

speaker: ALEX
text: After you complete the Chapter 5 tasks, Completing Chapter 5: Submit Your Evidence tells you to go back to your assigned Challenge 2 or Challenge 3 issue and post a comment with proof. For screen reader users navigating by keyboard, this part is important: swap in the actual issue numbers where you see [number].

speaker: ALEX
text: This is where the conversation shifts from idea to action. Expected Outcomes does three things: names the concept, gives you a move to try, shows what counts as proof. The checkpoints you should hear:

speaker: ALEX
text: Student can create an issue with a clear title and description. Student can communicate in issue threads using @mentions. Student can organize work by breaking issues into sub-issues.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Now it sounds like a workflow, not a pile of instructions.

speaker: ALEX
text: That confidence comes not from never getting confused, but from knowing how to find your footing again when you do.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Now If You Get Stuck. What should they take from that section?

speaker: ALEX
text: If You Get Stuck serves three purposes: it names the problem, gives you a practical move, and shows what success looks like. Here are the stops: Can't find a classmate's issue? Use is:open in the filter and look for recent ones. @mention not triggering? Make sure you type @ directly followed by the username - no spaces. Sub-issue option missing? Check with a facilitator - it might need to be turned on for this repository. Still stuck? Ask the facilitator for a direct issue link. Pause after each attempt and listen for the change before trying the next thing.

speaker: JAMIE
text: What's the real point?

speaker: ALEX
text: Step one: finished but unsure you got it right? Compare yourself against the Challenge 2 reference solution or the Challenge 3 reference solution. The goal isn't speed - it's never losing track of where you are.

speaker: ALEX
text: Before you move on, hold this: issues are collaborative spaces, not just to-do lists. This is where workflows become powerful because results become visible and explainable. An @mention says "pay attention to this thread." Sub-issues turn vague work into checkboxes. That's the gap between following steps and owning your process.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Let's look at Learning Pattern Used in This Chapter. What do learners need?

speaker: ALEX
text: Learning Pattern Used in This Chapter has the same structure: name the concept, give you something to do, show what proof looks like.

speaker: ALEX
text: The learning path: start small and safe by creating an issue; practice speaking up publicly by @mentioning a peer; organize bigger work by carving it into sub-issues; leave clear marks in the issue timeline so you can point to them. Every step should be visible and nameable.

speaker: JAMIE

speaker: ALEX
text: This chapter builds momentum for file editing and PR work coming in Chapter 6. If something feels off, stop and re-orient.

speaker: ALEX
text: Here's the piece people usually skip over: this chapter includes learning cards - expandable sections that give guidance tailored to how different people work. Not every card shows at every step.

text: What should someone know before they start typing?

speaker: ALEX
text: This is where Local Git Alternative: Working from Your Clone comes in. If you cloned the learning-room during Block 0 and prefer working on your computer instead of the web, this is for you.

speaker: ALEX
text: Treat these as spoken recipes, not decoration. You might hear cd /Documents/learning-room or wherever you cloned it; git status should show "On branch main". View your assigned challenge issues with gh issue list --assignee @me --label challenge. Look at a specific issue with gh issue view 42. Leave a comment with gh issue comment 42 --body "I'd like to try this!". Create an issue interactively with gh. Read it first, understand what it changes, then run it only when your repository state matches.

speaker: JAMIE
text: That level of precision keeps screen reader users on track.

speaker: ALEX
text: Exactly. The named thing - heading, tab, field, branch, button - that's your handhold.

speaker: ALEX
text: A solid Git practice is tracking three things: which branch you're on, what's changed, and what confirmation you should see before the next command runs.

speaker: ALEX
text: This is where the whole section clicks into place. Anchor on What Is a GitHub Issue? An issue is a discussion thread tied to a repository. In practice: every issue has a number like 42, a state (Open or Closed), a title, a description, and a comment thread. The skill isn't memorizing one screen - it's knowing how to reorient yourself when the display changes.

speaker: ALEX
text: Listen for the types in this list. Bug reports - "This feature doesn't work when using NVDA with Firefox". Feature requests - "Add a keyboard shortcut to jump to the next unread issue". Questions - "Can I assign an issue to myself, or only someone else?". Ideas - "Wouldn't it be useful if closed issues faded to lower contrast." These examples show what real issues sound like.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Now let's talk about Navigating to the Issues List. What's the entry point?

speaker: ALEX
text: From a repository page: you're on the repo home and see the tabs at the top - Code, Issues, Pull requests, etc. Activate the Issues tab.

speaker: ALEX
text: Direct URL: github.com/owner/repo/issues takes you straight there.

speaker: ALEX
text: The learning card - Navigating to the Issues List - covers these entry points with screen reader testing and keyboard paths specific to each route.

speaker: ALEX
text: Next section: The Issues List Page. This is where information gets announced. The page structure is: a filter bar at the top where you search and narrow; a list of issues below, each one showing the title, some metadata, and how old it is; sorting options; and a New issue button.

speaker: ALEX
text: How to read the issue list: each row announces the issue title, whether it's open or closed, how many comments, when it was updated, and who it's assigned to. The key is that every issue shows the title first - that's the core signal.

speaker: ALEX
text: What gets announced per issue: start with the title, then the state - open or closed - then optional labels, then assignee if there is one, then comment count and last update.

speaker: ALEX
text: The learning card - The Issues List Page - breaks this down with specific screen reader output and keyboard navigation paths.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Filtering and Searching Issues. How do people narrow their view?

speaker: ALEX
text: Using the search or filter bar: that text box near the top of the Issues tab. Type into it and use qualifiers. Useful queries include is:open, is:closed, label:bug, assignee:me, author:username, milestone:v2.0. You can combine them: is:open label:bug assignee:me finds open bugs assigned to you.

speaker: ALEX
text: Using the filter buttons: buttons to the left or above the search box that let you toggle Open, Closed, or filter by other criteria without typing.

speaker: ALEX
text: Open vs Closed filter: the distinction is simple but critical. Open means active work. Closed means resolved or won't-fix.

speaker: ALEX
text: Learning cards - Filtering and Searching Issues - show the exact announcements a screen reader makes for each filter option and fast keyboard paths to jump between states.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Reading an Issue. What happens when you land on one?

speaker: ALEX
text: Landing on an issue page: you see the title as a heading, then the author and timestamp, then the issue body, then comments and activity below. That's the reading order.

speaker: ALEX
text: Quick navigation: press 1 to jump to the title; press 3 to move between heading level 3 items if there are multiple sections; press G then I to get back to the Issues list from anywhere.

speaker: ALEX
text: Reading the issue description: the body can have Markdown - code blocks, lists, links. Read it the same way you'd read any document.

speaker: ALEX
text: Reading comments and activity: scroll down and you'll hear each comment in chronological order. Each one shows the author, timestamp, and the comment text. Some lines show events - "user closed this issue" or "user linked this to PR 42" - those are important context.

speaker: ALEX
text: Learning cards - Reading an Issue - detail how these are announced and the fastest keyboard routes to jump between comments.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Leaving a Comment. Walk us through that.

speaker: ALEX
text: Step one: scroll to the comment box at the bottom of the issue - it's a text field where you write. Step two: type your comment using Markdown if you want formatting. Step three: activate Comment or press Ctrl+Enter. Step four: listen for the page reload and confirmation that your comment posted.

speaker: ALEX
text: Markdown formatting while typing: the comment field announces when it recognizes Markdown syntax. You can use bold, italics, code blocks, lists, and links - the same as anywhere else on GitHub.

speaker: ALEX
text: GitHub shortcuts for the Issues page. On the Issues list page: G then I gets you there from anywhere; K shows all keyboard commands. On an open issue: P to jump to previous issue, N to jump to next issue, R to reply, L to toggle a label, A to assign.

speaker: ALEX
text: Learning cards - Leaving a Comment - provide the complete keyboard route and screen reader announcement for each action.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Filing a New Issue. That's the main skill. How do people start?

speaker: ALEX
text: Navigating to New Issue: from the Issues list page, look for the green New issue button - it's prominent at the top. Activate it.

speaker: ALEX
text: Filling Out the Issue Form. Title field: type a specific, descriptive title. At least 12 characters. Say what's wrong or what's missing, not just "Bug" or "Question".

speaker: ALEX
text: Description or Body field - this is where you give context. Here's the template most issues follow:

speaker: ALEX
text: "What happened" - the problem you ran into, the unexpected behavior, what went wrong.

speaker: ALEX
text: "What I expected" - the behavior that should have happened instead.

speaker: ALEX
text: "How to reproduce" - numbered steps anyone can follow to see the problem themselves. Be specific about versions, browser, screen reader, operating system.

speaker: ALEX
text: "Environment" - your setup details. Browser version, screen reader, OS, any relevant configuration.

speaker: ALEX
text: "Additional context" - anything else that might help. Screenshots, error messages, similar issues.

speaker: ALEX
text: This structure isn't rigid - adapt it for what makes sense. The goal is giving maintainers enough information to act without needing to ask clarifying questions.

speaker: ALEX
text: Assigning labels from the sidebar: the right side panel has a Labels section. Click or tab to it and activate labels that fit - "bug", "documentation", "enhancement", "good first issue". These tag your issue so people can filter and find it.

speaker: ALEX
text: Submitting the issue: find and activate the Submit or Create issue button. Listen for the page change and confirmation that your issue was created.

speaker: ALEX
text: Learning cards - Filing a New Issue - provide the announcements and keyboard navigation for every field and button.

speaker: ALEX
text: Tool card - File a New Issue - is a quick reference for the whole process.

speaker: JAMIE
text: Cross-Referencing Issues. What does that mean?

speaker: ALEX
text: Closing keywords in PR descriptions or issue comments: write "fixes #42" or "closes #150" and when your PR merges, it automatically closes that linked issue. The system recognizes these: closes, closed by, fix, fixes, fixed by, resolve, resolves, resolved by.

speaker: ALEX
text: Mentioning another issue in a comment: type #42 anywhere and it becomes a link. The issue timeline shows that the reference was made. This creates a visible trail between related work.

speaker: ALEX
text: Cross-repo references: #owner/repo#42 links to issue 42 in a different repository. Useful when work spans multiple projects.

speaker: ALEX
text: Now we zoom back. Why does all this matter? Issues are how open source maintainers, contributors, and users coordinate. Filing a good issue - clear title, rich description, appropriate labels - is how you help maintainers decide what to work on next. Reading issues carefully before you jump in is how you avoid duplicating work. Commenting thoughtfully is how you become a collaborator instead of just a reporter.

speaker: JAMIE
text: So the skill is not just the mechanics of clicking and typing.

speaker: ALEX
text: Right. The skill is learning to think like a collaborator. Before you create an issue, you're mentally asking: is this clear enough that someone who wasn't there can understand it? Before you comment, you're asking: does this add information or does it just take up space? That judgment grows over time, and this chapter gives you the safe space to practice.

speaker: ALEX
text: One more thing before we wrap. Carry the map. Know what page you're on, know what you're trying to do, and know what change should happen next. When the change doesn't show up, pause. That pause is not wasted time - it's professional practice, and it's how workflows transform from stressful to reliable.

speaker: JAMIE
text: That's the real lesson inside the steps.

speaker: ALEX
